blocks.text: The curve of Fig 19.1 also shows that the binding energy per nucleon increases up to A = 50. So when two light nuclei merge to form a heavier nucleus with mass number below 50, energy is given out. For example, when two protons and two neutrons merge to form a helium nucleus, about 27 MeV is given out.

blocks.title: Fusion reaction
blocks.text: A fusion reaction is a nuclear reaction in which two light nuclei merge to form a heavier nucleus.

In a fusion reaction some mass is lost and its equivalent energy is given out; more energy per nucleon can be obtained than in fission. But fusion is more difficult to produce: two positively charged nuclei must be brought very close together, which needs work against their electrostatic repulsion, so a very large amount of energy must be spent to start the reaction. The most probable fusion reactions of light nuclei are 2-1-H + 2-1-H -> 3-1-H + 1-1-H + 4.0 MeV (19.6) and 2-1-H + 2-1-H -> 3-2-He + 1-0-n + 3.3 MeV (19.7). In both of these reactions, about 1.0 MeV of energy per nucleon is produced, which is equal to the energy produced during fission. If deuterium (2-1-H) and tritium (3-1-H) are forced to fuse, 17.6 MeV is obtained: 2-1-H + 3-1-H -> 4-2-He + 1-0-n + 17.6 MeV (19.8). Deuterium and tritium are called fusion fuels.

blocks.alt: Two deuterium nuclei (each a proton and a neutron) collide to give a tritium nucleus (two neutrons and a proton) and a proton that flies off (4.0 MeV). Then the tritium nucleus and another deuterium nucleus collide to give a helium nucleus (two protons, two neutrons) and a neutron that flies off (17.6 MeV). A key shows neutron, proton, deuterium, tritium and helium.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.6: Fusion reaction (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.6).

blocks.text: To fuse two light nuclei, work must be done against their repulsion, so they are made to collide at very high speed. One method is to give the nuclei a very large velocity with an accelerator (Fig 19.6); it has been used to study the fusion of deuterium and tritium but cannot give continuous energy on a large scale. Another method uses the fact that the speed of atoms increases with temperature. The temperature needed is about 10 million degrees Celsius; the reaction at such a temperature is called a thermonuclear reaction. Such temperatures cannot ordinarily be reached, but they occur for a very short time in the explosion of an atom bomb, which is how the hydrogen bomb is triggered. Fusion has not yet been controlled like fission, so it is not yet used to produce electricity, though research continues. Fusion is taking place in the core of the Sun and other stars.

blocks.title: For your information: an 'artificial Sun'
blocks.text: An 'artificial Sun' refers to experimental fusion reactors such as China's EAST (an advanced superconducting tokamak) and HL-2M/HL-3. They use strong magnetic fields to confine hydrogen isotopes heated to over 100 million degrees, hotter than the Sun's core, in an attempt to fuse them into helium and release clean energy.
